stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the Clark's nutcracker and the agouti. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Clark's nutcracker is a bird found in the mountains of western North America.
• Each season it caches up to 30,000 whitebark pine seeds in the soil.
• Seeds the nutcracker buries but never recovers can sprout, helping the pine spread.
• The agouti is a rodent found in Central and South American rainforests.
• It buries Brazil nut seeds at scattered spots across its territory.
• Seeds the agouti buries but never recovers can sprout, helping Brazil nut trees spread.
choices: Whereas the Clark's nutcracker caches whitebark pine seeds in western mountains, the agouti buries Brazil nut seeds in tropical rainforests.
Both the Clark's nutcracker, a bird, and the agouti, a rodent, help trees spread when seeds they bury but never recover later sprout.
The Clark's nutcracker caches up to 30,000 whitebark pine seeds each season, and the ones it fails to retrieve can sprout.
Like the Clark's nutcracker, which caches up to 30,000 seeds per season, the agouti buries tens of thousands of seeds each year.
explanation: The two blocks of notes differ on type of animal, region, and tree species, but they share one feature: seeds each animal buries and never recovers sprout and help a tree spread. Choice B states that shared feature for both animals and marks the similarity with 'both.'

A.why: You picked an accurate, detailed sentence, but it's built on 'whereas.' It points out how the two animals differ in region and seed, which is the opposite of emphasizing a similarity.

C.why: This choice describes the shared behavior for the nutcracker only. It never mentions the agouti, so it can't show that the two animals have anything in common.

D.why: This choice does set up a similarity, but the notes never say how many seeds the agouti buries. The 30,000 figure applies only to the nutcracker, so 'tens of thousands' for the agouti goes beyond the notes.

stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between Lepidodendron and Glossopteris. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Lepidodendron was a tree-sized relative of club mosses that grew in coal swamps about 330 million years ago.
• It could reach 40 meters tall.
• Its fossil roots were first named as a separate genus, Stigmaria, before they were found attached to Lepidodendron trunks.
• Glossopteris was a woody seed plant that grew across the southern continents about 270 million years ago.
• It is best known from tongue-shaped leaves found in Antarctica, India, and Africa.
• Its fossil roots were first named as a separate genus, Vertebraria, before they were linked to Glossopteris leaves.
choices: Lepidodendron grew in coal swamps about 330 million years ago, whereas Glossopteris grew across the southern continents about 270 million years ago.
Both Lepidodendron and Glossopteris are best known today from tongue-shaped leaves found in Antarctica, India, and Africa.
Lepidodendron's fossil roots were first named as a separate genus, Stigmaria, before being found attached to the 40-meter-tall plant's trunks.
The fossil roots of both Lepidodendron and Glossopteris were first classified as separate genera before being recognized as parts of those plants.
explanation: The plants differ in age, habitat, and size, but the last note in each block matches: each plant's fossil roots were first named as a separate genus and only later connected to the plant. Choice D states this for both plants and uses 'both' to mark the similarity.

A.why: Every fact here is accurate, but 'whereas' sets the two plants against each other by age and setting. That emphasizes a difference, not a similarity.

B.why: This choice is phrased as a similarity, but it gives Glossopteris's tongue-shaped leaves to Lepidodendron as well. The notes say nothing like that about Lepidodendron, so the shared feature it claims isn't actually shared.

C.why: This choice picks up the right feature, roots first named as a separate genus, but describes it only for Lepidodendron. It never says Glossopteris had the same history, so no similarity is shown.

stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between Osei's and Brandl's work. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Mirela Osei is a Ghanaian-British printmaker.
• She makes woodcuts, carving her images into plywood salvaged from demolished buildings.
• Her prints depict crowded market scenes in Accra.
• Tomas Brandl is an Austrian printmaker.
• He makes drypoints, scratching his images into flattened juice cartons collected from cafés.
• His prints depict empty valleys in the Alps.
choices: Osei and Brandl both make their prints from discarded materials, working on salvaged plywood and used juice cartons, respectively.
Osei's woodcuts depict crowded market scenes in Accra, while Brandl's drypoints show empty valleys in the Alps.
Osei, a Ghanaian-British printmaker, carves her woodcuts into plywood salvaged from buildings that have been demolished.
Like Osei's woodcuts, Brandl's drypoints depict scenes from the region in which the artist has lived since childhood.
explanation: The two artists differ in nationality, technique, and subject, but each prints from a surface someone threw away: salvaged plywood for Osei and used juice cartons for Brandl. Choice A names that shared feature for both artists and marks it with 'both.'

B.why: You went with a vivid, accurate sentence, but 'while' sets up a contrast between busy markets and empty valleys. The goal asked for a similarity, and this choice highlights a difference.

C.why: This choice states Osei's use of discarded material but never mentions Brandl. A similarity needs both artists, so describing only one doesn't do the job.

D.why: This choice sounds like a similarity, but the notes never say where either artist lives or for how long. It invents a shared feature the notes don't support.

stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the findings of the two studies. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 2019, economist Lena Furtado studied a minimum-wage increase in Portugal's retail sector.
• She compared employment in 850 shops before and after the increase.
• She found that employment did not fall.
• In 2021, economist Daniel Okafor studied a minimum-wage increase in Nigeria's construction sector.
• He analyzed payroll records from 300 firms.
• He found that employment did not fall, though workers' average weekly hours dropped by 4 percent.
choices: Furtado studied 850 Portuguese retail shops in 2019, whereas Okafor examined payroll records from 300 Nigerian construction firms in 2021.
Furtado and Okafor both found that a minimum-wage increase left the number of jobs and workers' weekly hours unchanged.
Furtado and Okafor both found that employment did not fall after a minimum-wage increase, in Portuguese retail and Nigerian construction, respectively.
Okafor found that employment in Nigerian construction did not fall after a minimum-wage increase, though average weekly hours dropped 4 percent.
explanation: The notes are in research order for each study, and the goal points you to the findings. The one finding the studies share is that employment did not fall after the wage increase. Choice C states that result for both economists and marks it with 'both.'

A.why: This choice compares the studies' methods, years, and settings rather than their findings, and 'whereas' frames even those as differences. It misses the goal twice.

B.why: This choice is phrased as a shared finding, but Okafor found that weekly hours dropped by 4 percent. Saying hours stayed the same in both studies goes against the notes, which makes this the closest wrong answer.

D.why: This choice reports the shared result for Okafor's study only. Furtado never appears, so the sentence can't show that the two studies agree.

stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between DAS and smartphone-based networks. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) detects earthquakes using fiber-optic cables.
• The cables were originally laid to carry internet and telephone traffic.
• DAS can record ground motion at points spaced a few meters apart along a cable.
• Smartphone-based networks detect earthquakes using the accelerometers inside ordinary phones.
• The accelerometers were originally built to rotate screens and count steps.
• Smartphone networks can reliably detect only quakes of magnitude 4.5 or above.
choices: DAS detects earthquakes using fiber-optic cables, which were originally laid to carry internet and telephone traffic.
DAS and smartphone networks both detect earthquakes with equipment built for other purposes: communication cables and phone accelerometers.
DAS records ground motion at points a few meters apart, whereas smartphone networks reliably detect only quakes of magnitude 4.5 or above.
Both DAS and smartphone networks detect earthquakes by recording ground motion at points spaced only a few meters apart.
explanation: Each block's second note says the same kind of thing: the equipment was first built for something other than seismology, cables for communication and accelerometers for screen rotation and step counting. Choice B states this for both methods and marks the similarity with 'both.'

A.why: This choice picks up the right feature, repurposed equipment, but only for DAS. It never says smartphone networks share it, so no similarity is shown.

C.why: The details are accurate and specific, but 'whereas' contrasts the two methods' capabilities. That emphasizes a difference, not a similarity.

D.why: This choice is phrased as a similarity, but the meter-scale spacing belongs to DAS alone. The notes say nothing of the kind about smartphone networks, so the claimed shared feature isn't shared.

stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity in the two birds' feeding behavior. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The kiwi is a bird native to New Zealand.
• It forages mainly at night.
• It locates earthworms and insects by smell, using nostrils at the tip of its long bill.
• The kakapo is a parrot also native to New Zealand.
• Weighing up to 4 kilograms, it is the world's heaviest parrot.
• It is active mainly at night, when it feeds on seeds, fruit, and plants.
choices: The kiwi locates earthworms and insects by smell, whereas the kakapo feeds on seeds, fruit, and plants.
Both native to New Zealand, the kiwi and the kakapo eat very different foods: animal prey and plant matter, respectively.
The kakapo, the world's heaviest parrot, searches for seeds, fruit, and plants mainly at night.
The kiwi and the kakapo, two birds native to New Zealand, both search for food mainly at night.
explanation: The goal asks for a similarity in feeding behavior. Before reading the choices, look for the feeding fact the two blocks share: both birds look for food mainly at night. Choice D names both birds and uses 'both' to attach that one shared trait to the pair. That is exactly the job the goal sets.

A.why: This is about feeding, but 'whereas' sets up a contrast between the two diets. You picked a detailed feeding sentence without checking whether it shows a similarity or a difference.

B.why: The word 'Both' drew you in, but the shared fact here is where the birds live, not how they feed. The main clause actually stresses a difference in their diets.

C.why: This is the shared trait, night feeding, but it is stated only for the kakapo. The sentence never says the kiwi also feeds at night, so no similarity is shown.

stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity in how mangrove forests and salt marshes affect coastlines. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Mangrove forests grow along tropical coastlines.
• Some mangrove trees can exceed 20 meters in height.
• Their dense, arching roots slow incoming tides, causing sediment to settle.
• Salt marshes are grassy wetlands found mainly along temperate coastlines.
• Marsh grasses rarely grow taller than 2 meters.
• Their stiff stems slow incoming tides, causing sediment to settle.
choices: Whereas mangrove forests grow along tropical coastlines, salt marshes are found mainly along temperate ones.
In both mangrove forests and salt marshes, plant structures slow incoming tides, causing sediment to settle.
Some mangrove trees can exceed 20 meters in height, but marsh grasses rarely grow taller than 2 meters.
In mangrove forests, dense, arching roots slow incoming tides, causing sediment to settle along the shore.
explanation: The goal asks for a similarity in how the two habitats affect coastlines. In both blocks, plants slow the tides and make sediment settle: roots in one case, stems in the other. Choice B states that effect once and applies it to both habitats with 'both', so the similarity is named outright.

A.why: This is accurate, but 'Whereas' marks a difference in location, not a similarity in effect. You chose a sentence that sets the two habitats against each other.

C.why: The heights are given for both habitats, but 'but' turns them into a contrast, and height is not an effect on the coast. You were drawn by the precise numbers.

D.why: This describes the right effect, but only for mangroves. Salt marshes never come up, so nothing tells the reader the two habitats work the same way.

stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between Europa and Enceladus. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Europa is a moon of Jupiter.
• Its diameter is about 3,100 kilometers.
• Scientists have concluded that a liquid-water ocean lies beneath its icy crust.
• Enceladus is a moon of Saturn.
• Its diameter is about 500 kilometers.
• Geysers at its south pole spray water vapor and ice grains into space.
• Scientists have concluded that a liquid-water ocean lies beneath its icy crust.
choices: Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, sprays water vapor and ice grains into space from geysers at its south pole.
At about 3,100 kilometers across, Europa is more than six times as wide as Enceladus, which measures about 500.
Europa and Enceladus are both moons whose icy crusts, scientists have concluded, cover liquid-water oceans.
Europa orbits the planet Jupiter, whereas Enceladus, a moon about 500 kilometers across, orbits Saturn.
explanation: Of the two blocks, only one line repeats word for word: scientists have concluded that each moon has a liquid-water ocean under an icy crust. Choice C names both moons and uses 'both' to give them that one feature, which emphasizes a similarity.

A.why: The water geysers make this feel connected to the oceans, but the sentence covers only Enceladus. It never says Europa shares any feature with it.

B.why: This compares the two moons precisely, but the comparison shows a difference in size. A detailed comparison is not a similarity.

D.why: 'Whereas' signals a contrast. This sentence shows the moons orbit different planets, which is a difference, not a similarity.

stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the sound systems of Hawaiian and Rotokas. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The average language uses about 22 consonant sounds.
• Hawaiian is a Polynesian language spoken in Hawaii.
• It uses 8 consonant sounds.
• Rotokas is a language spoken on the island of Bougainville in Papua New Guinea.
• It uses 6 consonant sounds, among the fewest of any known language.
choices: Hawaiian and Rotokas each use far fewer consonant sounds than the average language, which uses about 22.
Rotokas uses 6 consonant sounds, two fewer than the 8 used by Hawaiian, a Polynesian language.
Hawaiian is spoken in Hawaii, but Rotokas is spoken on the island of Bougainville in Papua New Guinea.
With only 6 consonant sounds, Rotokas uses among the fewest consonants of any known language.
explanation: Hawaiian has 8 consonant sounds and Rotokas has 6. The average language has about 22, so both are far below it. Choice A uses 'each' to give that shared trait to both languages and uses the average as the benchmark that makes the similarity clear.

B.why: Both languages' sound systems appear here, which makes this tempting. But 'two fewer than' measures the gap between them, so the sentence stresses a difference.

C.why: 'But' sets up a contrast, and the contrast is about where the languages are spoken, not about their sound systems. This misses the goal twice.

D.why: This gives the small consonant count for Rotokas only. It never says Hawaiian also has very few consonants, so no similarity is shown.

stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the outcomes of the two training programs. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Exercise physiologist Ana Ferreira's team compared two eight-week training programs for recreational cyclists.
• Group 1 rode short, all-out sprint intervals, training about 1.5 hours per week.
• Group 1's aerobic capacity rose by 10 percent.
• Group 2 took long, moderate-paced rides, training about 5 hours per week.
• Group 2's aerobic capacity rose by 10 percent.
• Group 1 riders rated their sessions as more physically uncomfortable.
choices: The sprint-interval riders trained about 1.5 hours per week, whereas the long-ride riders trained about 5 hours.
Riders in the sprint-interval and long-ride programs alike saw their aerobic capacity rise by 10 percent.
Ferreira's sprint-interval riders raised their aerobic capacity by 10 percent while training only 1.5 hours weekly.
Riders in the sprint-interval program rated their sessions as more uncomfortable than long-ride riders did.
explanation: The notes follow research order, and the goal points to the results stage. The result the groups share is that both raised their aerobic capacity by 10 percent. Choice B names both programs and uses 'alike' to join them under that one outcome.

A.why: Weekly training time is part of the method, not an outcome, and 'whereas' frames it as a contrast. You chose a parallel-looking sentence that points to a difference.

C.why: This states the right outcome but only for the sprint group. The word 'only' even hints at a contrast without naming the long-ride group's matching result.

D.why: This compares the two groups, but on discomfort, where they differed. Comparing two items is not the same as emphasizing what they share.
